title: Basal Ganglia Gas and Brake
description: A simplified, textbook-standard basal ganglia circuit (cortex, striatum D1 and D2 neurons, GPe, subthalamic nucleus, GPi/SNr, thalamus, and dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta). A dopamine slider changes the strength of the direct (GO) and indirect (NO-GO) pathways and moves a movement-output meter from hypokinetic (Parkinson-like) through normal to hyperkinetic.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: Neuroscience
Motor Control
Basal Ganglia
Dopamine
Parkinson's Disease
learningObjectives: Explain how a change in dopamine shifts the balance between the direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways.
Predict whether movement output will be too little (hypokinetic), normal, or too much (hyperkinetic) for a given dopamine level.
Identify each connection in the classic basal ganglia loop as excitatory (glutamate) or inhibitory (GABA).
prerequisites: Excitatory versus inhibitory neurotransmitters, including glutamate, GABA, and dopamine (Chapter 3)
Location of the basal ganglia, thalamus, and motor cortex (Chapter 4)
keyQuestions: Why does inhibiting an inhibitor (disinhibition) release movement?
How can dopamine excite one group of striatal neurons and inhibit another, yet push both pathways toward more movement?
Why does losing dopamine neurons in Parkinson's disease make movement slow and hard to start?
Why can too much dopamine signaling cause extra, unwanted movements?
misconceptions: Dopamine simply 'turns on' muscles. In fact it adjusts the balance of a brake-release circuit in the basal ganglia.
Inhibition always means less movement. In the direct pathway, inhibiting the GPi/SNr brake produces more movement.
More dopamine is always better. Too much dopamine signaling weakens the brake and lets unwanted movements through.
The two-pathway model is the complete wiring diagram. It is a simplified teaching model that leaves out other connections.

controls.label: Dopamine (% of normal)
controls.purpose: Sets dopamine release from the substantia nigra pars compacta.

equations: Zones: output < 0.35 too little; 0.35 to 0.65 normal; > 0.65 too much
simulationModel.assumptions: All activities are on an illustrative 0 to 1 scale, with every node at 0.5 when dopamine is normal. Cortical input is constant.
simulationModel.limitations: Leaves out the hyperdirect pathway, feedback loops, timing, firing patterns, and the many non-motor loops of the basal ganglia. Numbers are not measured data.
